sections.title: Start here: Kerala Real Estate Business
sections.summary: What the course covers, how it works, the legal and ethics rules, and the course map. 22 modules, 53 lessons, 22 weeks part-time.
sections.content:
## What this course is

A practical course in running a legal, honest real estate service business in Kerala, written for a beginner near Kuttiady, Kozhikode, with an Android phone, an old laptop, ₹0 for learning and very little capital. It focuses first on **low-capital paths**: brokerage, rentals and property management, NRI property care and real estate marketing. Buying property to invest is treated as a later stage.

By the end you will understand how a property deal works from token advance to registration and mutation, be able to do due diligence and valuation, know the main Kerala and central laws, run your service with written agreements, and have either **closed a first real deal** (a rental or a sale) legally, or produced a complete investment analysis and business plan.

## What you will be able to do

- Convert cents, ares and square feet; read survey numbers, thandaper, certificates, EC and deeds.
- Explain the main laws (Transfer of Property Act, Registration Act, stamp duty, RERA, paddy land, land reforms, building rules, CRZ, ESA, rent control, benami, cash limits) and when each matters.
- Run a full due-diligence checklist and know exactly when to bring in an advocate or surveyor.
- Value property with comparables, fair value and income methods; calculate the full cost of buying, rental yield, cap rate, cash-on-cash and IRR.
- Understand TDS, capital gains, rental income tax and GST at the level a broker needs (and when to call a CA).
- Register as an agent if required, take written mandates, source, market, negotiate and manage transactions and rentals.
- Spot the common frauds in Kerala and protect your clients.

## Duration

- **22 modules, 53 lessons** in three parts; lessons take 10 to 25 minutes to read, plus a real-world task in your local market.
- **Part-time:** 22 weeks at about 5 to 6 hours a week (about 100 hours), alongside PSC preparation.
- **Full-time:** about 9 calendar weeks at about 15 hours a week. The capstone deal needs real calendar time.

## The three parts

Each part works on its own; its part page says what to set up if you start there.

| Part | Modules | Part-time weeks | Study time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A: Understand the business** | Modules 1–2 | 1–1 | about 6 h |
| **B: Knowledge base** | Modules 3–9 | 2–8 | about 33 h |
| **C: Run the business** | Modules 10–22 | 9–21 | about 51 h |

## How every lesson works

Core lesson with a Kozhikode or Kerala example → worked calculation where numbers matter → key rules with the date checked and the source → when you need a licensed professional → free resources (what to study, how long) → an action task in your local market with proof → a copy-ready template → common mistakes → a local fraud warning → a short quiz with answers → a progress checklist. Each module has a project, a rubric, a "short on time" version, flashcards and tools for your **Real Estate Toolkit**.

## Legal, accuracy and ethics

**This course is educational only. It is not legal, tax or investment advice.** Property law, rates, fees and portals change; every rule in this course is dated "as of November 2026" and marked "check current rules". Before any real transaction, check the official source and use licensed professionals: an **advocate** for title opinions and legal disputes, a **licensed surveyor** for measurement and boundary questions, a **chartered accountant** for tax, and a **licensed document writer or advocate** to draft deeds. Never do work that needs a licence you don't hold. This course never recommends a specific property or investment; it teaches you how to evaluate them.

**Ethics rules you follow in every task:** act only with the owner's consent (written for listings); never misrepresent a property; follow K-RERA rules; avoid cash and black-money dealings; respect clients' privacy (blur ID numbers and phone numbers in anything you share).

**Honest risk warning:** property is illiquid (it can take months or years to sell), legal disputes are common and slow, prices can stagnate or fall, and many small investors lose money through bad titles, unapproved layouts, over-borrowing and fraud. This course shows you how to reduce those risks, not how to avoid them completely.

## Key assumptions made for this course

- No real estate course existed in the app, so this is a new course with stable IDs (RE-M01-L01 and so on).
- You will start with a service business (brokerage, rentals, NRI care, marketing) and treat buying to invest as later.
- Rates and rules were checked on 2026-11-04; the Kerala Registration, Revenue and Ente Bhoomi portals block automated checks, so for them the course gives the official addresses and cross-checks details with secondary guides, clearly marked.
- From 1 April 2026 the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the 1961 Act, and many section numbers changed; the course explains tax rules by what they do and names old and new numbers only where checked.
- Topics covered by other courses in this app are cross-referenced: sales skills in [Entrepreneurship](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/entrepreneurship/ent-m07) (in the Practical Entrepreneurship course), social media in [Social Media Marketing](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/social-media-marketing/smm-m11) (in the Practical Social Media Marketing course), and investing basics in [Personal Finance](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/personal-finance/fin-m08) (in the Practical Personal Finance for India course).
- All names in examples are fictional.

## The course map

| Module | What it covers | What you build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M01 | Property types, players, cycles, Kerala demand drivers | A local market snapshot |
| M02 | Broker, rentals, NRI care, marketing, plotting, investing, flipping | Your chosen path with risks |

| M04 | TPA, Registration Act, stamp duty, RERA, paddy land, land reforms, building rules, CRZ, ESA, rent control, benami, cash limits | A one-page legal map |
| M05 | Agreement for sale, sale deed, gift, partition, settlement, POA, rental, permits, OC, NOCs | Annotated sample documents |
| M06 | Title chain, EC, litigation, physical checks, flood and zoning, professionals | A full due-diligence run |
| M07 | Fair value vs market value, comparables, income and cost methods | 20+ listing comparables sheet |
| M08 | Loans, EMI, yield, cap rate, cash-on-cash, IRR, total cost | ROI analysis of 5 properties |
| M09 | TDS, capital gains, rent tax, GST, brokerage income tax | A tax checklist for buyers, sellers and you |
| M10 | K-RERA agent registration, mandates, commission, inventory | A mandate template and 5 inventory entries |
| M11 | Local, NRI, builder and online sourcing; broker interviews | Interview notes and a sourcing plan |
| M12 | Photos, video, virtual tours, listings, portals, social, WhatsApp, GBP | A real listing, live |
| M13 | Client needs, site visits, objections, negotiation, closing, token | A site visit and a negotiation plan |
| M14 | Token to agreement, loans, stamp duty, SRO registration, mutation, handover | A transaction timeline |
| M15 | Tenant screening, agreements, verification, rent, maintenance, NRI care | A rental management package |
| M16 | Layouts, conversion, roads, utilities, development risk | A development feasibility screen |
| M17 | Cost per sq ft, contracts, quality checks, permits | A construction cost estimate |
| M18 | Rentals, land banking, flipping, REITs, risks | An investment comparison |
| M19 | CRM in Sheets, Google Earth, QGIS, AI | A working CRM and a map of your listings |
| M20 | Structure, registration, GST, bookkeeping, pricing, partnerships | A one-page business setup plan |
| M21 | Fake titles, double sales, forged POAs, encroachment, black money, ethics | A fraud checklist and ethics code |
| M22 | A first legal deal, or an investment analysis plus business plan | Your complete toolkit |

## Start here

1. Read the **Weekly schedule**.
2. Do **Week 0: setup** (about 1 hour) and the **Baseline quiz** (20 minutes).
3. Start Module 1 in week 1 and the **Weekly market track** (20 minutes every Sunday).

sections.summary: Create your Real Estate Workbook in Google Sheets or LibreOffice, your toolkit folders, saved portal links and your local study area.
sections.content:
About one hour. Everything is free.

## The free tool stack

- **Google Sheets** (phone app) or **LibreOffice Calc** (laptop): your **Real Estate Workbook** with the tabs below.
- **Google Drive** or a phone folder called **Real Estate Toolkit**, with sub-folders: 00 Setup, 01 How real estate works in Kerala, 02 Business paths and choosing yours … 22 Capstone: your first deal or your business plan.
- **Phone camera** and a free video editor for listings (Module 12).
- **Google Maps / Google Earth** for locations and rough measurements; [QGIS](https://qgis.org/) on the laptop later (Module 19).
- **WhatsApp Business** (free) for client communication, if you choose (Module 12).
- A **notebook** for office visits and interviews.

## Workbook tabs

| Tab | Added in | Row 1 headings or contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Comps | Module 7 | `Date seen,Source (portal/broker/owner),Link or contact,Locality,Panchayat/municipality,Type (land/house/flat/commercial),Land area (cents),Built-up area (sq ft),Asking price (Rs),Price per cent (Rs),Price per sq ft (Rs),Road frontage (ft),Road width (ft),Distance to town (km),Flood/slope notes,Status (asking/sold/withdrawn),Notes` |
| Cost | Module 4 | Full cost of a purchase (calculator) |
| ROI | Module 8 | Rental yield and return calculator |
| Leads | Module 19 (start earlier if you get leads) | `Lead ID,Date,Name,Phone,Source,Buy/Rent/Sell/Let,Type,Area wanted,Budget (Rs),Stage (new/contacted/visit booked/visited/offer/agreement/closed/lost),Next action,Next action date,Properties shown,Notes,Consent (Y/N)` |
| Inventory | Module 10 | Properties you have a mandate for |
| Log | Week 1 | Weekly market log numbers |

## Steps

1. Create the workbook and folders.
2. Add the **Log** tab and the Sunday reminder for the weekly market log.
3. Save the official portal addresses in your phone browser: K-RERA, Kerala Registration, IGR fair value, Revenue (ReLIS), Ente Bhoomi, e-Rekha, KSDMA hazard maps (links in Modules 3 and 4).
4. Write down your **local area**: the panchayats and towns you will study (for example Kuttiady, Velom, Kayakkody, Maruthonkara, Kunnummal, Nadapuram and Kozhikode city). Changing these names for your own area is fine.
5. Decide your privacy rule: you never post anyone's ID, phone number or documents publicly, and you blur personal details in screenshots.

sections.title: Baseline quiz: where you start
sections.summary: A 12-question knowledge quiz (form A) and a 10-item skills self-rating. You repeat both at the end with form B.
sections.content:
Take this in week 0 and write your scores in the **Log** tab. You will take form B at the end. Don't worry about a low score: that is the point of a baseline.

## Knowledge quiz, form A (12 questions, 15 minutes)

Answer without looking anything up; guessing is fine. Score 1 per correct answer, out of 12. Cover the answers first.

1. How many square feet are in one cent?
    - A) About 435.6 sq ft
    - B) 100 sq ft
    - C) 1,000 sq ft
    - D) 4,356 sq ft
2. One are equals about how many cents?
    - A) 10 cents
    - B) 1 cent
    - C) 0.5 cents
    - D) About 2.47 cents
3. What does an encumbrance certificate (EC) mainly show?
    - A) Registered transactions on the property, such as sales and mortgages, for the period searched
    - B) The government fair value
    - C) That the property has no flood risk
    - D) That the building has a permit
4. A seller says "the agreement for sale is enough; we don't need a sale deed." What is true?
    - A) An agreement for sale transfers ownership
    - B) A notarised agreement is the same as registration
    - C) Only flats need a sale deed
    - D) Ownership passes only by a registered sale deed; an agreement for sale does not transfer ownership
5. As of November 2026, what are the usual stamp duty and registration fee for a sale deed in Kerala?
    - A) 5% and 5%
    - B) A fixed Rs 5,000
    - C) 1% and 1%
    - D) Stamp duty 8% and registration fee 2% of the higher of price or fair value
6. Who must register with K-RERA under the RERA Act?
    - A) Real estate agents who facilitate sales in registrable projects, and promoters of such projects
    - B) Only banks
    - C) Only buyers
    - D) Nobody in Kerala
7. Land shown in the paddy and wetland data bank:
    - A) Is always government land
    - B) Cannot be freely filled or built on; conversion needs legal approval and may not be allowed
    - C) Can be built on after paying land tax
    - D) Is the best land for a quick house
8. A buyer pays Rs 60 lakh for a house. Who deducts TDS, and roughly how much?
    - A) The seller pays 10%
    - B) No TDS on houses
    - C) The bank pays 5%
    - D) The buyer deducts 1% (about Rs 60,000) and deposits it for the seller
9. A house costs Rs 40 lakh and rents for Rs 12,000 a month. What is the gross rental yield?
    - A) About 3.6%
    - B) About 12%
    - C) About 30%
    - D) About 0.3%
10. Which is the safest way to take a token advance?
    - A) In cash with a verbal promise
    - B) By bank transfer, with a signed receipt stating the terms
    - C) Through the broker's personal cash
    - D) In cash with no receipt
11. When is an advocate's title opinion most important?
    - A) Only for flats
    - B) After registration
    - C) Never, the EC is enough
    - D) Before signing the agreement for sale and paying a large advance
12. Which is a warning sign of a possible fraud?
    - A) The seller asks for payment by bank transfer
    - B) The seller insists on a quick cash deal through a power of attorney holder and refuses to show originals
    - C) The seller provides a 30-year EC
    - D) The seller asks for an advocate to check the title

### Answers, form A

1. **A.** One cent is one-hundredth of an acre: 43,560 ÷ 100 = 435.6 sq ft (RE-M03-L01).
2. **D.** One are is 100 square metres, about 2.47 cents (RE-M03-L01).
3. **A.** An EC lists registered transactions; it does not prove there are no unregistered claims or court cases (RE-M06-L01).
4. **D.** Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act (RE-M04-L01).
5. **D.** Check current rules before every deal (RE-M04-L01).
6. **A.** Agents need registration and must quote the number (RE-M10-L01).
7. **B.** The Kerala Conservation of Paddy Land and Wetland Act (RE-M04-L03).
8. **D.** TDS applies when the consideration or stamp duty value is Rs 50 lakh or more (RE-M09-L01).
9. **A.** Rs 12,000 × 12 = Rs 1.44 lakh; ÷ Rs 40 lakh = 3.6% (RE-M08-L02).
10. **B.** Cash limits and proof matter (RE-M13-L02, RE-M04-L05).
11. **D.** Due diligence comes before commitment (RE-M06-L03).
12. **B.** Forged or misused powers of attorney are a common fraud (RE-M21-L01).

sections.summary: A 20-minute Sunday market log, plus milestones: 20+ comparables, fair-value checks, broker interviews, a due-diligence run, ROI for 5 properties, a real listing, a CRM and a site visit.
sections.content:
Two things run underneath the course: a **weekly market log** (20 minutes every Sunday) and a set of **practical milestones** that build your local knowledge and your toolkit. **This week** on the course page shows each one when it is due.

## The weekly market log

Every week, add about three real listings to your Comps sheet, meet or call at least one new person in the property world, update your leads, and check one rule or rate on an official source.

```
WEEKLY MARKET LOG (Sunday, 20 minutes)          Week ___
1. Listings added to the Comps sheet this week: ___ (target 3)
2. New contacts: brokers ___ owners ___ buyers/tenants ___ professionals ___
3. Leads in CRM: new ___ ; follow-ups done ___ ; overdue ___
4. One thing I learned about how deals work here: ______________________
5. One rule or rate I checked on an official source (with date): ______
6. Next week's three actions: 1 ______ 2 ______ 3 ______
```

## Milestones

| Due by week | Milestone | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Part A review | half a page on what you learned in Part A and what you will do next |
| 5 | Due-diligence checklist run on a real property (with permission) or the sample case | the filled checklist |
| 6 | Market study: 10 real listings in your Comps sheet | the Comps sheet with 10 rows |
| 6 | Market study: 20+ real listings (land and houses), price per cent and per sq ft | the Comps sheet with 20+ rows and the summary cells |
| 7 | Fair value looked up on the official portal for 3 properties and compared with asking prices | screenshots or notes with dates |
| 8 | Rental yield and ROI analysis for 5 real properties | the ROI tab with 5 properties |
| 8 | Part B review | half a page on what you learned in Part B and what you will do next |
| 10 | Interviews: 3 local brokers and 1 document writer or advocate | your interview notes |
| 10 | One real listing (with the owner's written permission) posted on free portals and social media | the owner's permission, the listing links and screenshots |
| 11 | A real site visit conducted or shadowed | your site-visit checklist |
| 14 | CRM sheet in use: every lead tracked with next action dates | a CRM screenshot with personal details blurred |

## Rules for field work

- Always ask permission before photographing a property or a person; get the owner's **written** permission before listing.
- Visit offices politely, during working hours, and never pretend to be a buyer or an officer.
- Don't collect or share anyone's personal documents. Use your own property or a family property (with permission) for record practice, or the sample case in the course.

Every copy-ready tool in one place. Copy them into your workbook or toolkit folder; the lesson named under each explains how to use it.

## Comparables sheet with formulas

sections.content:
*Part A: Understand the business.*

## Overview

Before learning laws and documents, you need a picture of the market you will work in. This module is mostly field work: a road survey, conversations and a one-page snapshot that you will update throughout the course.

Remember the course rule from **Start here**: this is education, not legal, tax or investment advice. You will learn when to call an advocate, a surveyor, a CA or a document writer, and never to do their licensed work yourself.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Classify properties by type and by legal land type.
- Name the players in a deal and what each is responsible for.
- Describe market cycles and Kerala's demand drivers.
- Write a one-page snapshot of your local market.

## Time

About 2 hours 45 minutes in total: 2 hours of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: week 1, with the module project due in week 1.

## Lessons

1. RE-M01-L01: Property types and the people in a deal (about 1 hour)
2. RE-M01-L02: Market cycles and what drives demand in Kerala (about 1 hour)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The local players map and property-type count (RE-M01-L01).
- The local market snapshot (RE-M01-L02).

## Module project: a local market snapshot and players map

1. Complete the road survey and players map (RE-M01-L01).
2. Complete the market snapshot (RE-M01-L02).
3. Share the snapshot with one experienced person (a broker or a relative who has bought land) and note what they disagree with.
4. Save both in your toolkit folder; you will update the snapshot at the end of Part B and in the capstone.

**Proof to record:** Your players map, road survey count, market snapshot and the feedback note.

## Add to your Real Estate Toolkit

Save these in your toolkit folder and Google Sheets workbook (set up in Week 0). By the capstone they form your complete business toolkit.

- Local players map (offices, document writers, advocates, surveyors, banks, brokers).
- Local market snapshot, version 1.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Property types | Confuses legal and physical type | Knows main types | Classifies by physical and legal type with examples |
| Players | Few named | Most roles named | All roles named with local offices and contacts |
| Market drivers | Generic list | Some local evidence | Local evidence from conversations, infrastructure and hazard maps |
| Honesty | Repeats "prices only go up" | Some caveats | Separates asking prices from real deals and names risks |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study or work leaves little time:

- Do the road survey on one short stretch (5 properties).
- Write a half-page snapshot from one conversation.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, say the answer aloud, then check.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Purayidam | Garden or dry land in revenue records; generally buildable. |
| Nilam | Paddy or wet land; protected by law. |
| Who registers deeds? | The Sub-Registrar Office. |
| Who drafts deeds? | A licensed document writer or an advocate. |
| Who gives a title opinion? | An advocate. |
| Four cycle stages | Recovery, expansion, peak/oversupply, slowdown. |
| Main Malabar demand driver | NRI remittances. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Skipping field work.** Your local knowledge is your main asset as a beginner.
- **Treating rumours as data.** Write down sources and dates.
- **Overlooking rentals.** Rentals are often the fastest low-capital start.

sections.title: RE-M01-L01: Property types and the people in a deal
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can classify any Kerala property by type, name everyone involved in a typical deal and what each is paid for, and map the players in your own area. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 40 minutes of field notes).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

**Property types you will meet in Kerala:**

- **Land (plots):** the most traded asset in rural and semi-urban Kerala. Recorded in revenue records by land type: **purayidam** (garden or dry land, generally buildable), **nilam** (paddy or wet land, protected by law, RE-M04-L03), **thottam** or plantation land, and others. A plot's legal type matters more than how it looks today.
- **Residential:** independent houses (the most common), villas in gated projects, flats/apartments (mostly in towns and cities such as Kozhikode, Kochi and Thiruvananthapuram), and rooms or portions let to tenants.
- **Commercial:** shop rooms (very common on town roads and junctions), office spaces, godowns, hotels and lodges, petrol pumps, hospitals and schools.
- **Agricultural:** coconut, arecanut, rubber and mixed farmland; paddy fields.
- **Plantation:** large holdings of rubber, tea, coffee, cardamom or pepper, mostly in the hills; land reforms law gave plantations special treatment, so converting plantation land to other uses can be legally sensitive (RE-M04-L03).
- **Special categories:** government-assigned (pattayam) land with restrictions, temple or trust land, puramboke (government) land, and land in coastal (CRZ) or ecologically sensitive areas.

**Who is involved in a typical deal:**

| Player | Role | How they are paid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner/seller | Holds title; signs the deed | Sale price |
| Buyer | Pays; usually needs a loan or NRI funds | — |
| Broker/agent | Finds the other side, arranges visits, helps negotiate and coordinate | Commission, often a percentage (local norms vary; RE-M10-L02) |
| Document writer | Licensed to draft deeds; prepares the sale deed and handles registration paperwork | Fee per document |
| Advocate | Gives the legal title opinion, handles disputes and complex documents | Fee |
| Licensed surveyor | Measures land and fixes boundaries | Fee |
| Sub-Registrar Office (SRO) | Registers the deed; collects stamp duty and fees | Government revenue |
| Village office and taluk | Keep revenue records; issue certificates; mutation | Government fees |
| Local body (panchayat/municipality) | Building permits, building numbers, building tax | Fees and taxes |
| Bank or housing finance company | Lends; does its own legal and technical checks | Interest and fees |
| Builder/developer | Builds and sells flats, villas or plots | Margin |

Your business will sit among these players, so knowing what each one does (and does **not** do) is the first skill. A broker who tries to act as an advocate or document writer risks breaking the law and harming clients.

## Local example

Sachin's neighbour, Kunhammed, wants to sell 15 cents of purayidam with an old house on the Kuttiady–Thottilpalam road to fund his daughter's studies. The buyer is a nurse working in Kuwait who wants a plot to build on later, close to her parents in Velom.

In the deal: a local broker who knows both families; a document writer near the Kuttiady SRO who drafts the deed; an advocate in Vadakara engaged by the buyer's brother to check title; the village office, which issues the possession certificate and later records the mutation; the SRO, where the deed is registered; and a bank in Kozhikode that gives the buyer a loan against her salary. The buyer is abroad, so she signs a registered power of attorney in favour of her brother (RE-M05-L02).

Seven parties, at least five offices or professionals, and many places where things can go wrong. A good broker coordinates them; a bad one hides problems to close quickly.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala Real Estate Regulatory Authority (K-RERA): agent and project registration, complaints, project search](https://rera.kerala.gov.in/) | Browse the project search: see which project types (apartments, villas, plots, commercial) are registered in Kozhikode district | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04; check current rules |
| [Wikipedia: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Estate_%28Regulation_and_Development%29_Act,_2016) | Read the summary of who RERA covers (promoters, agents, buyers) | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [NoBroker: list your property for rent or sale (free for owners)](https://www.nobroker.in/list-your-property-for-rent-sale) | Look at how property types and sizes are listed (no account needed for browsing) | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04; check current rules |

## Action task (in your local market)

1. Walk or ride one main road in your area (for example Kuttiady town to Thottilpalam) and note at least 15 properties by type: land, house, flat, shop, commercial building, farmland, plantation.
2. Note every property sign you see ("For sale", "For rent", broker boards) with the phone number (for your private records only).
3. List the players in your area by name or office: nearest SRO, village office, panchayat office, two banks, document writers near the SRO, two advocates, any builders.
4. Write three lines: which property type you see most for sale, which for rent, and which seems hardest to sell.

**Proof to record:** A note with 15+ properties by type, the sign board count, your local players list and the three-line summary.

## Template: Local players map

```

Brokers seen (boards, ads): 1 ______ 2 ______ 3 ______
Builders / developers: 1 ______
PROPERTY TYPE COUNT (one road survey)

```

## Common mistakes

- **Judging land by how it looks.** A green, dry plot may still be nilam in records. Legal type comes from the records, not the eye.
- **Thinking a broker can do everything.** Title opinions are for advocates, deeds for licensed document writers or advocates, measurement for surveyors.
- **Ignoring commercial and rental demand.** Shop rooms and rentals often move faster than land and suit a low-capital start.

## Local fraud warning

**"Clear title, ready for registration" boards.** Some sellers and brokers advertise land as "clear" without any check. A board or a WhatsApp message is not evidence. Until you have seen the deed, a 30-year EC and an advocate's opinion, treat every claim as unverified (Module 6).

## Quiz

Answer from memory first. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which land type in Kerala revenue records is generally buildable?
    - A) Forest land
    - B) Purayidam (garden or dry land)
    - C) Nilam (paddy land) in the data bank
    - D) Puramboke (government land)
2. Who is licensed to draft a sale deed?
    - A) Any broker
    - B) A licensed document writer or an advocate
    - C) The buyer's bank
    - D) The village officer
3. Where is a sale deed registered?
    - A) At K-RERA
    - B) At the village office
    - C) At the panchayat
    - D) At the Sub-Registrar Office (SRO)
4. What does the village office handle in a deal?
    - A) Revenue records, certificates and mutation
    - B) Building permits
    - C) Home loans
    - D) Stamp duty collection

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and browse K-RERA project search
- **Action:** survey one road for 15+ properties and map your local players. It is done when your proof is saved: a note with 15+ properties by type, the sign board count, your local players list and the three-line summary.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Purayidam is dry land; nilam and puramboke have strong restrictions.
2. **B.** Deed drafting is licensed work; brokers coordinate but don't draft.
3. **D.** The SRO registers documents and collects stamp duty and fees.
4. **A.** Building permits are the local body's job; stamp duty goes through the SRO.

sections.title: RE-M01-L02: Market cycles and what drives demand in Kerala
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can explain what drives property demand and prices in Kerala, recognise the stage of a market cycle, and write a short snapshot of your local market. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 40 minutes of research and conversations).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

**Property markets move in cycles.** A simple four-stage picture:
1. **Recovery:** after a slump, few deals, prices flat, sellers patient.
2. **Expansion:** demand grows (jobs, remittances, new roads), deals pick up, prices rise, new projects launch.
3. **Peak/oversupply:** prices outrun incomes, many unsold flats and plots, speculation ("prices only go up").
4. **Slowdown:** deals dry up, sellers cut asking prices quietly, builders offer discounts, some projects stall.

Real markets are messier, and Kerala's land market can stay "frozen" for years: owners keep asking old prices, few deals happen, and real prices are hidden. That is why you will track **actual** listings and, where you can, actual sale prices (Module 7).

**What drives demand in Kerala:**
- **NRI money (remittances):** Gulf and other overseas earnings have long funded house building and land purchases, especially in Malabar. When Gulf jobs or oil prices weaken, local demand often softens.
- **Migration and demographics:** young people moving to cities or abroad; ageing parents in large houses; small families wanting smaller, low-maintenance homes; migrant workers from other states needing cheap rentals.
- **Infrastructure:** new or widened roads (national highway widening, bypasses), railway improvements, airports (Kozhikode airport at Karipur is nearby), hospitals, colleges and IT parks raise nearby values; announcements move prices before work starts, sometimes too much.
- **Tourism:** homestays and resorts near beaches, backwaters and hill areas (Wayanad, Munnar, Kozhikode beaches), subject to CRZ, ESA and local rules.
- **Education and healthcare clusters:** demand for rentals near medical colleges and universities.
- **Interest rates and loan availability:** lower rates make loans cheaper and lift demand.
- **Disasters and climate risk:** the 2018 and 2019 floods and landslides changed what buyers ask about; flood history now affects value (RE-M06-L02).
- **Law and policy:** fair-value increases, stamp duty changes, paddy-land conversion rules and building rules all affect deals.

**Good questions for any local market:** Who is buying here (NRIs, local salaried, investors, migrants)? What are they buying (plots, houses, flats, shops)? How long do listings stay up? Are sellers cutting prices? What is changing nearby (roads, colleges, rules)?

## Local example

In 2025 and 2026, brokers around Kuttiady describe a market like this (the course's fictional summary of common patterns; check your own area): demand for small residential plots of 5 to 10 cents near the town and main roads from NRIs and salaried families; slow demand for large plots in interior areas without good road access; strong rental demand for small houses and rooms from teachers, government staff and migrant workers; and almost no flats outside Kozhikode city.

Prices on roads leading to Kozhikode and near the bypass are higher per cent than interior roads, and plots with a history of water-logging in the 2018 monsoon now sell more slowly. Your task is to replace this fictional summary with real notes from your own conversations and listings.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala Real Estate Regulatory Authority (K-RERA): agent and project registration, complaints, project search](https://rera.kerala.gov.in/) | Count how many registered projects you can find in Kozhikode district by type; note any near you | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04; check current rules |
| [Kerala State Disaster Management Authority: hazard maps (flood, landslide)](https://sdma.kerala.gov.in/hazard-maps/) | Open the hazard maps and find the flood and landslide maps for Kozhikode district | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [MIT OpenCourseWare 11.431J Real Estate Finance and Investment (Geltner and McGrath, CC BY-NC-SA)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/11-431j-real-estate-finance-and-investment-fall-2006) | Optional: read the first lecture note on real estate markets (space and asset markets) | 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task (in your local market)

1. Talk to three people about the local property market (a relative who bought recently, a shopkeeper, a broker). Ask the five questions: who buys, what, how long listings stay, price cuts, what is changing nearby.
2. Find one infrastructure project or plan near you (a road widening, a bypass, a college, a hospital) and note its stage (announced, land acquisition, construction, complete).
3. Check the KSDMA flood and landslide hazard maps for your panchayat and note whether parts of your area are marked.
4. Write a one-page market snapshot: main demand drivers, cycle stage (your best guess), property types in demand, and risks.

**Proof to record:** Notes from three conversations, one infrastructure note, a hazard-map note and your one-page market snapshot.

## Template: Local market snapshot

```
LOCAL MARKET SNAPSHOT                    Area: ______  Date: ______
Who is buying: NRIs __ local salaried __ investors __ migrants/tenants __
What sells fastest: ______   What sells slowest: ______
Typical listing time (from conversations): ______
Price trend (rising / flat / falling / frozen): ______  Evidence: ______
Demand drivers here: remittances / roads / colleges / hospitals / tourism / other ______
Infrastructure nearby (stage): ______
Hazards (KSDMA maps, 2018/2019 flood history): ______
My guess at the cycle stage: recovery / expansion / peak / slowdown. Why: ______
Opportunities for a low-capital service business: ______
```

## Common mistakes

- **Believing "land prices never fall".** Real prices can stagnate or fall for years, especially for interior and flood-prone land.
- **Taking asking prices as market prices.** Asking prices are often far above what deals close at. Track listings and ask about actual deals.
- **Buying on infrastructure announcements.** Projects get delayed or re-routed. Check the stage before treating it as value.

## Local fraud warning

**"New road coming" land sales.** Sellers sometimes claim a highway or bypass will pass next to a plot to justify a high price. Ask for the official alignment or notification, check the stage, and remember that land acquired for the road itself may be acquired at notified compensation, not market hopes.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which has historically been a major driver of land and house demand in Malabar?
    - A) Mining
    - B) Large manufacturing industries
    - C) Remittances from Kerala workers abroad, especially in the Gulf
    - D) Government land auctions
2. What is a sign that a market is in a slowdown?
    - A) Banks raise loan limits
    - B) Buyers compete for every plot
    - C) New projects launch every month
    - D) Listings stay up longer and sellers quietly cut prices
3. Why track actual listings and deals rather than what people say?
    - A) Asking prices and talk often differ from real closing prices
    - B) Talk is always lies
    - C) Banks require it
    - D) Listings never change
4. How did the 2018 and 2019 floods affect the Kerala market?
    - A) Flood-prone land became more expensive
    - B) Buyers now ask about flood history, and flood-prone plots can sell more slowly
    - C) They had no effect
    - D) All prices doubled

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and look at the KSDMA hazard maps for your district
- **Action:** talk to three people, note an infrastructure project and write a one-page market snapshot. It is done when your proof is saved: notes from three conversations, one infrastructure note, a hazard-map note and your one-page market snapshot.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** NRI money has long funded house building and land purchases.
2. **D.** Longer listing times and price cuts signal weaker demand.
3. **A.** Real data protects your clients and your reputation.
4. **B.** Hazard history now affects demand and value.

sections.title: Module 2: Business paths and choosing yours
sections.summary: Business paths in real estate: brokerage, rental brokerage, property management, NRI property care, marketing and consulting (low capital), and plotting, buy-and-hold, flipping and land banking (high capital), with the money, skills, risks and time to income of each, and honest numbers on why small investors often lose money.
sections.content:
*Part A: Understand the business.*

## Overview

You choose your starting path here. With little capital and 5 to 7 hours a week, the course recommends starting with services (often rental brokerage plus NRI property care, or marketing) and treating investing as a later stage.

This decision is not final: you will revisit it in Module 18 (investing) and Module 22 (capstone).

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Compare all real estate paths by capital, skills, risk and time to income.
- Explain with numbers why small investors often lose money.
- Calculate a break-even price for a flip.
- Choose one or two starting paths with three next steps.

## Time

About 2 hours 45 minutes in total: 2 hours of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: week 1, with the module project due in week 1.

## Lessons

1. RE-M02-L01: Low-capital paths: brokerage, rentals, NRI property care, marketing (about 1 hour)
2. RE-M02-L02: Capital-heavy paths: plotting, buy-and-hold, flipping (about 1 hour)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The path chooser (RE-M02-L01).
- The flip break-even calculator (RE-M02-L02).

## Module project: your chosen path with risks and a 90-day start plan

1. Complete the path chooser (RE-M02-L01) and the break-even calculation (RE-M02-L02).
2. Write a one-page 90-day plan for your chosen path: services, target clients, first three steps, what you must learn first (which modules).
3. List the risks of your path and how you will reduce each.
4. Share the plan with one experienced person and note their comments.

**Proof to record:** The path chooser, the break-even calculation, your 90-day plan with risks, and the feedback.

## Add to your Real Estate Toolkit

Save these in your toolkit folder and Google Sheets workbook (set up in Week 0). By the capstone they form your complete business toolkit.

- Path chooser and 90-day start plan.
- Flip break-even calculator (Cost tab).

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Comparison | One path considered | Several paths scored | All paths compared with local evidence |
| Numbers | No calculation | Rough numbers | Break-even calculation on a real listing |
| Plan | Vague | Steps without dates | 90-day plan with steps, learning and risks |
| Honesty about risk | Ignores risks | Lists risks | Lists risks with ways to reduce each |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study or work leaves little time:

- Score the five low-capital paths and pick one.
- Write three first steps.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, say the answer aloud, then check.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Five low-capital paths | Sales brokerage, rental brokerage, property management, NRI property care, marketing. |
| Purchase transaction costs in Kerala (approx.) | About 10%+ (8% stamp duty, 2% registration, fees, brokerage); check current rules. |
| Why flips often fail | Costs, slow resale, taxes, holding costs. |
| Main risk of land banking | Money locked for years with no guarantee of rising prices. |
| When to consider investing | After an emergency fund, experience, a full analysis and money you can lock away. |
| Simpler property exposure | Listed REITs (Module 18). |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Following hype.** Use numbers and local evidence.
- **Skipping the written plan.** A 90-day plan turns a choice into action.
- **Mixing personal and client money.** Keep them separate from day one (Module 20).

sections.title: RE-M02-L01: Low-capital paths: brokerage, rentals, NRI property care, marketing
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can compare the low-capital real estate paths (brokerage, rentals, property management, NRI property care, marketing) by money, skills, risk and time to first income, and pick one or two to start. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 40 minutes of research and planning).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

With little capital, you earn in real estate by **providing services**, not by owning property. Five low-capital paths suit a beginner in Kerala:

**1. Sales brokerage.** You help owners sell and buyers buy, for a commission. Income per deal can be large, but deals are slow and many fail. You need a written mandate from the owner (RE-M10-L02), K-RERA registration where the law requires it (RE-M10-L01), and strong honesty, because buyers rely on what you say.

**2. Rental brokerage.** You find tenants for owners (or homes for tenants) for a fee, often a portion of one month's rent (local norms vary). Rentals move faster than sales and teach you the whole process: listing, visits, screening, agreements.

**3. Property management.** You manage rented properties for owners: rent collection, repairs, tenant issues, statements. Income is small but recurring (a percentage of rent or a fixed monthly fee).

**4. NRI property care.** Many Kerala homes are owned by people working abroad. They need someone trustworthy to visit, photograph, pay taxes and bills, arrange repairs, deal with tenants, and collect documents from offices. This is one of the best fits for a reliable beginner in Malabar (RE-M15-L02).

**5. Real estate marketing and content.** Owners and brokers need good photos, walkthrough videos, listing copy and social posts. If you build skill here (Module 12), you can serve many brokers and builders without handling transactions. The [Social Media Marketing course module on local business](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/social-media-marketing/smm-m11) (in the Practical Social Media Marketing course) covers the marketing side in depth.

**Consulting** (coordinating due diligence, helping buyers compare properties) becomes possible later, once you have deep knowledge and a network of advocates and surveyors. Be careful never to present yourself as giving legal opinions or formal valuations.

**How to choose:** list your strengths (trust in your community, photography, follow-up, office work), your time (5 to 7 hours a week now), your network (NRI families? landlords?), and the local demand you found in Module 1. Many people combine two paths, for example rental brokerage plus NRI property care.

## Local example

Sachin has five to seven hours a week, a phone, a motorbike and many relatives with family members in the Gulf. His options:

- **Rental brokerage** around Kuttiady: teachers and government staff are often posted to the area and need small houses; migrant workers need rooms. Owners often don't want the hassle of finding tenants.
- **NRI property care:** at least six families he knows have houses that stay empty or are rented informally while the owners work abroad. They worry about leaks, encroachment, unpaid taxes and tenants not paying.
- **Sales brokerage:** slower, needs more knowledge first.

He chooses rental brokerage plus NRI property care for the first six months, while studying the sales side. His first step is a written service menu (RE-M15-L02) and two conversations with NRI families during their next visit home.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kerala Real Estate Regulatory Authority (K-RERA): agent and project registration, complaints, project search](https://rera.kerala.gov.in/) | Read the agent registration section headings to see what registration involves | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04; check current rules |
| [NoBroker: list your property for rent or sale (free for owners)](https://www.nobroker.in/list-your-property-for-rent-sale) | Study how rental listings are presented and what owners must provide | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04; check current rules |

## Action task (in your local market)

1. Score each of the five low-capital paths 1–5 on: fits my time, fits my skills, local demand, my network, and risk (5 = low risk).
2. Talk to one owner (a landlord or an NRI family) and ask: "What is your biggest headache with your property?" Write the answer word for word.
3. Choose one or two paths and write a one-paragraph reason.
4. Write the first three concrete steps for your chosen path (for example: make a service menu, talk to five NRI families, list one rental).

**Proof to record:** Your scored comparison of the five paths, the owner's answer, your chosen path with reasons and three next steps.

## Template: Path chooser

```
PATH CHOOSER (score 1-5)       Time  Skills  Demand  Network  Risk(5=low)  Total
Sales brokerage                 __     __      __      __       __          __
Rental brokerage                __     __      __      __       __          __
Property management             __     __      __      __       __          __
NRI property care               __     __      __      __       __          __
Marketing / content             __     __      __      __       __          __
Owner's biggest headache (quote): "______________________"
My path(s): ______  Why: ______
First three steps: 1 ______ 2 ______ 3 ______
```

## Common mistakes

- **Starting with investing because it sounds bigger.** With little capital, services build income, knowledge and a network first.
- **Trying every path at once.** Pick one or two; do them well.
- **Underestimating trust.** NRI care and property management are trust businesses; one mistake with money ends them.

## Local fraud warning

**"Join our network, pay ₹10,000 to become a franchise broker."** Some schemes sell "real estate agent franchises" or "training with guaranteed leads". You don't need to pay anyone to start a legal service business; check any such offer with the red-flag check from the Mind, Body and People course (PD-M32-L01 there) and never pay for "guaranteed" income.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Why do low-capital paths suit a beginner?
    - A) They earn from services, so you don't need money to buy property
    - B) They are risk-free
    - C) They need no knowledge
    - D) They always pay the most
2. Which path gives small but recurring income?
    - A) Flipping
    - B) Land banking
    - C) Property management
    - D) One-off land sale brokerage
3. What must a broker never do?
    - A) Market a property honestly
    - B) Take a written mandate
    - C) Arrange site visits
    - D) Give legal title opinions or draft deeds without the required licence
4. Why is NRI property care a good fit in Malabar?
    - A) It needs a large investment
    - B) Many homes are owned by families working abroad who need trustworthy local help
    - C) NRIs never visit
    - D) It requires a law degree

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the path table
- **Action:** score the five low-capital paths, talk to one owner and choose your path with three next steps. It is done when your proof is saved: your scored comparison of the five paths, the owner's answer, your chosen path with reasons and three next steps.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Services build income, skill and network before investing.
2. **C.** Management fees recur monthly.
3. **D.** That work belongs to advocates and licensed document writers.
4. **B.** Demand plus low capital needs.

sections.title: RE-M02-L02: Capital-heavy paths: plotting, buy-and-hold, flipping
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can explain the capital, skills and risks of plotting, buy-and-hold investing, flipping and land banking, with honest numbers, and decide when (if ever) to move into them. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 35 minutes of calculation and notes).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

**Capital-heavy paths** involve buying property with your own money and usually loans. They can build wealth, but they also lose people money regularly. Here is the full comparison of all paths:

| Path | Capital needed | Key skills | Main risks | Time to income |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Broker / agent (sales) | Very low (phone, travel, K-RERA fee if required) | Local knowledge, networking, negotiation, documents | Irregular income; deals fall through; legal exposure if careless | 3–12 months to first sale |
| Rental broker | Very low | Tenant screening, agreements, quick follow-up | Small fees; tenant problems | Weeks |
| Property management | Low | Reliability, maintenance contacts, accounts | Owner and tenant disputes; money handling | 1–3 months |
| NRI property care | Low | Trust, reporting, office work, maintenance | Responsibility for others' assets; misuse of authority | 1–3 months |
| Real estate marketing / content | Low (phone, free tools) | Photography, video, copywriting, social media | Clients delay payment; competition | Weeks |
| Consulting (due-diligence coordination, valuation help) | Low | Deep knowledge plus professional network | Must not cross into licensed legal or valuation work | 6–12 months |
| Plotting and development | Very high | Land law, approvals, construction, finance | Approvals fail, money stuck, legal liability | Years |
| Buy-and-hold rentals | High (down payment, loan) | Analysis, tenant management | Low yields, vacancies, illiquidity, repairs | Years |
| Flipping | High | Buying below market, renovation, fast resale | Transaction costs (about 10%+), slow resale, taxes | 6–24 months per deal |
| Land banking | High | Patience, legal checks | Money locked for years; prices may not rise; encroachment | Years |

**Why small investors lose money in property:**
1. **Bad title or illegal land** (data bank paddy land, encroached land, unapproved layouts, disputed inheritance): the property can't be sold, built on or financed.
2. **Transaction costs:** in Kerala, buying costs roughly 10% or more on top of the price (8% stamp duty, 2% registration fee on the higher of price or fair value, plus document, legal and brokerage fees, RE-M04-L01). A flip must beat that before any profit.
3. **Illiquidity:** land in interior areas can take a year or more to sell, at a lower price than hoped.
4. **Low rental yields:** houses in Kerala often rent for well under 3% to 4% of their price a year, often less than a fixed deposit, before repairs and vacancies (RE-M08-L02).
5. **Over-borrowing:** EMIs continue even when tenants leave or prices fall.
6. **Disputes:** boundary, access-road and family disputes can take years in court.

**When to consider them:** after you have (a) an emergency fund and no high-interest debt (see [Personal Finance, emergency fund](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/personal-finance/fin-m05) (in the Practical Personal Finance for India course)), (b) a few years of service experience and a trusted advocate and surveyor, (c) a full analysis showing returns after all costs, taxes and risks (Module 18), and (d) money you can leave locked for years. For many people, low-cost listed REITs are a simpler way to get property exposure (RE-M18-L02).

## Local example

Sachin's cousin Rasheed wants to "flip" a 10-cent plot: buy at ₹18 lakh and sell within a year at ₹21 lakh.

Rough costs: stamp duty and registration on ₹18 lakh at 10% (assuming the fair value is not higher): ₹1.8 lakh; document writer, EC and other fees: about ₹25,000; brokerage at 1% on purchase: ₹18,000; brokerage at 1% on sale: ₹21,000. Total costs: about ₹2.44 lakh. Profit before tax: ₹21 lakh − ₹18 lakh − ₹2.44 lakh = **about ₹56,000**, about 3% on ₹18 lakh, before short-term capital gains tax, and only if he sells at ₹21 lakh within the year. If it takes two years to sell at ₹20 lakh, he loses money. Rasheed decides to keep his savings in his emergency fund and help with Sachin's rental work instead.

## Worked calculation

**Break-even price for a flip:**
- Purchase price P = ₹18,00,000
- Purchase costs (stamp duty 8% + registration 2% + fees + brokerage) ≈ 10% + ₹25,000 + 1% ≈ ₹2,23,000
- Sale costs (brokerage 1%) ≈ ₹21,000 at the target price
- Break-even sale price ≈ P + purchase costs + sale costs ≈ **₹20,44,000**, roughly 13.6% above the purchase price, before tax and holding costs (interest you could have earned, land tax, maintenance).
- In Google Sheets: `=B1*1.11+25000+B2*0.01` where B1 is the purchase price and B2 the target sale price (rates as of November 2026; check current rules).

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Square Yards (updated July 2026): stamp duty and registration charges in Kerala](https://www.squareyards.com/blog/stamp-duty-and-registration-charges-in-kerala) | Read the stamp duty and registration table to confirm the 8% + 2% used in the example | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 through a secondary source; check current rules |
| [MIT OpenCourseWare 11.431J Real Estate Finance and Investment (Geltner and McGrath, CC BY-NC-SA)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/11-431j-real-estate-finance-and-investment-fall-2006) | Optional: skim the syllabus to see how professionals think about real estate investment | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [The Week (30 June 2021): SEBI cuts minimum application amount for REITs](https://www.theweek.in/news/biz-tech/2021/06/30/sebi-reduces-minimum-application-amount-for-reits-should-you-invest-now.html) | Read how small investors can buy REIT units (more in RE-M18-L02) | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 through a secondary source; check current rules |

## Action task (in your local market)

1. Find one real land listing in your area. Calculate the purchase costs and the break-even resale price using the calculation above.
2. Ask one person who has bought land as an investment: "How long did it take to sell, and at what price compared with what you hoped?" Note the answer.
3. Write your rule for when you would consider a capital-heavy path (savings, experience, analysis, time).
4. Add your chosen low-capital path and your "later" rule to your toolkit folder.

**Proof to record:** One break-even calculation on a real listing, notes from one investor conversation and your written rule.

## Template: Flip break-even calculator

```
FLIP BREAK-EVEN (rates as of November 2026; check current rules)
B1 Purchase price (Rs)                     [type]
B2 Fair value (Rs)                         [type]
B3 Duty base                               =MAX(B1,B2)
B4 Stamp duty + registration (10%)         =B3*0.10
B5 Fees (document writer, EC, misc.)       [type]
B6 Brokerage on purchase                   =B1*[rate]
B7 Target sale price                       [type]
B8 Brokerage on sale                       =B7*[rate]
B9 Holding costs (interest lost, taxes, maintenance) [type]
B10 Break-even sale price                  =B1+B4+B5+B6+B8+B9
B11 Profit before tax at target price      =B7-B10
```

## Common mistakes

- **Ignoring transaction costs.** About 10% or more goes to costs on purchase; a flip must clear that first.
- **Counting the asking price as profit.** Use realistic sale prices and times from real deals.
- **Using emergency money or loans for land speculation.** Money locked in illiquid land can't help you in an emergency.

## Local fraud warning

**"Guaranteed doubling" land and plot schemes.** Ads promising that a plot will double in value in two or three years, often in "upcoming" layouts far from town, are a classic trap. Unapproved layouts may never get permits or roads (RE-M16-L01). No one can guarantee property returns.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. About how much do stamp duty and registration add to a Kerala sale deed, as of November 2026?
    - A) About 25%
    - B) Nothing
    - C) About 10% (8% + 2%) of the higher of price or fair value
    - D) About 1%
2. Why do many small property investors lose money?
    - A) Property always rises
    - B) Bad titles, high transaction costs, illiquidity, low yields and over-borrowing
    - C) Banks pay their EMIs
    - D) Taxes are zero
3. What should you have before investing in property?
    - A) A tip from a friend
    - B) An emergency fund, no high-interest debt, experience, a full analysis and money you can lock away
    - C) A guaranteed-return scheme
    - D) A credit card
4. A flip bought at ₹18 lakh needs roughly what sale price to break even?
    - A) About ₹20.4 lakh after costs
    - B) ₹18.5 lakh
    - C) ₹30 lakh
    - D) ₹18 lakh

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the path comparison table
- **Action:** calculate the break-even resale price for one real listing and write your rule for capital-heavy paths. It is done when your proof is saved: one break-even calculation on a real listing, notes from one investor conversation and your written rule.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Plus document, legal and brokerage costs; check current rules.
2. **B.** These risks are common and often ignored.
3. **B.** Investing comes after financial safety and skill.
4. **A.** Purchase and sale costs add roughly 13.6%.

sections.content:
*Part B: Knowledge base.*

## Overview

Part B, the knowledge base, starts with the records that every deal depends on. A good broker reads land papers quickly and spots mismatches; that one skill prevents most bad deals.

Practise on your own family's papers (with permission) or the sample case in RE-M06-L03. Never ask strangers for their documents for practice.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Convert land and building units and explain area types.
- Read survey and resurvey numbers, thandaper, tax receipts, sketches and certificates.
- Explain what revenue records prove and what they don't.
- Use the official land-record portals safely.

## Time

About 4 hours 15 minutes in total: 3 hours 15 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: week 2, with the module project due in week 2.

## Lessons

1. RE-M03-L01: Cents, ares and square feet: measuring land and buildings (about 1 hour)
2. RE-M03-L02: Survey numbers, thandaper and village office certificates (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. RE-M03-L03: Online land-record portals (about 1 hour)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The area conversion sheet (RE-M03-L01).
- The land records comparison (RE-M03-L02).
- The portal guide and fair value log (RE-M03-L03).

## Module project: a land-records walk-through for one plot

1. Choose one plot you can legally check (your family's, with permission).
2. Complete the area comparison (RE-M03-L01), the records comparison (RE-M03-L02) and the fair value search and EC walk-through (RE-M03-L03).
3. Write a one-page summary: what matches, what doesn't, what you'd ask an advocate or surveyor.
4. Save your conversion sheet and portal guide in the toolkit.

**Proof to record:** The three comparisons, the summary and your portal guide (personal details masked).

## Add to your Real Estate Toolkit

Save these in your toolkit folder and Google Sheets workbook (set up in Week 0). By the capstone they form your complete business toolkit.

- Units tab with conversion formulas.
- Land records comparison template.
- Portal guide with official addresses and fair value log.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Units | Errors in conversion | Mostly right | Fast, accurate conversions with formulas |
| Records | Can't read papers | Reads most items | Reads and cross-checks every item |
| Portals | Not used | Some used | Fair value, EC and land tax portals used with notes |
| Judgement | Treats tax receipts as title | Knows the limits | Explains what each record proves and when to call a professional |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study or work leaves little time:

- Learn the five unit conversions.
- Search one fair value on the official portal.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, say the answer aloud, then check.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 cent | 435.6 sq ft = 40.47 sq m. |
| 1 are | 100 sq m = 2.471 cents. |
| Carpet vs super built-up | Usable inside area vs built-up plus a share of common areas. |
| Correlation statement | Links old survey numbers to resurvey numbers. |
| Thandaper | Landholder's account in village revenue records. |
| Possession certificate | Supports possession; does not prove title. |
| EC portal | PEARL (Kerala Registration). |
| Fair value | Government minimum value for stamp duty; often below market. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Skipping the paperwork practice.** Reading papers is the core skill.
- **Assuming online records are always right.** Cross-check with deeds and offices.
- **Doing a surveyor's or advocate's job.** Know your limits.

sections.title: RE-M03-L01: Cents, ares and square feet: measuring land and buildings
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can convert between cents, ares, acres, hectares, square feet and square metres, estimate a plot's area from its measurements, and explain carpet, built-up and super built-up area. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 40 minutes of practice and a field measurement).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

**Kerala land units.** In everyday Kerala deals, land is priced **per cent**. Official records after the resurvey use **ares** and **hectares** (metric), and older deeds may use cents and acres. Buildings are measured in **square feet** (sq ft) in the market and **square metres** in building rules and permits.

| Unit | Square feet | Square metres | Other |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 cent | 435.6 sq ft | 40.47 sq m | 0.405 are |
| 1 are | 1,076.4 sq ft | 100 sq m | 2.471 cents |
| 1 acre | 43,560 sq ft | 4,046.9 sq m | 100 cents = 40.47 ares |
| 1 hectare | 1,07,639 sq ft | 10,000 sq m | 100 ares = 247.1 cents = 2.471 acres |
| 1 sq m | 10.764 sq ft | 1 sq m | 0.0247 cent |

**Quick memory rules:** 1 cent ≈ 436 sq ft ≈ 40.5 sq m. 1 are ≈ 2.47 cents. 10 cents ≈ 4,356 sq ft ≈ 4.05 ares. 1 acre = 100 cents.

**Estimating area from measurements.** For a roughly rectangular plot, area = length × width. For irregular plots, split the shape into rectangles and triangles (area of a triangle = ½ × base × height) and add them. On the ground, measure with a tape (or count paces only as a rough check). For any boundary question or legal measurement, a **licensed surveyor** must measure; your estimate is only for your own understanding.

**Building areas** (important when comparing houses and flats):
- **Carpet area:** the usable floor area inside the walls (rooms, kitchen, toilets). Under RERA, builders must quote prices on carpet area for registered projects.
- **Built-up area:** carpet area plus the thickness of walls and, often, balconies.
- **Super built-up area:** built-up area plus a share of common areas (lobbies, stairs, lifts). Flats in Kerala cities were often sold on super built-up area before RERA; super built-up can be 20% to 35% more than carpet area, which makes the price per sq ft look lower than it is.
- **Plinth area:** the covered area at the floor level, used in some building-rule and tax contexts.

Always ask: **which area** is this price per sq ft based on?

## Local example

A listing in Kayakkody says "8.25 cents, ₹2.2 lakh per cent". The deed shows **3.34 ares**. Check: 3.34 × 2.471 = 8.25 cents. ✓ Price: 8.25 × ₹2,20,000 = **₹18,15,000**.

A house nearby is advertised as "1,450 sq ft, ₹48 lakh". The owner's building permit shows 118 sq m plinth area: 118 × 10.764 = 1,270 sq ft. The extra 180 sq ft in the advert is a sit-out and a sunshade counted generously. The real price per sq ft of the house on the permit area is ₹48,00,000 ÷ 1,270 ≈ **₹3,780**, not ₹3,310 as the advert implies (and that price also includes the land).

## Worked calculation

**Irregular plot:** a plot is 30 m along the road, 45 m deep on the left side and 38 m deep on the right side (a trapezium).
- Area ≈ (45 + 38) ÷ 2 × 30 = 41.5 × 30 = **1,245 sq m**
- In ares: 1,245 ÷ 100 = **12.45 ares**
- In cents: 1,245 ÷ 40.47 ≈ **30.8 cents**
- In Google Sheets: cents from sq m `=A1/40.4686`; cents from ares `=A1*2.47105`; sq ft from cents `=A1*435.6`.
This is an estimate only. A licensed surveyor's measurement and the official sketch decide the legal area.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [e-Rekha (Kerala Land Information Mission): buy digital survey records and maps](https://erekha.kerala.gov.in/) | Look at the list of record types and prices (maps, FMB, area list) to see how areas are recorded | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04; check current rules |
| [Wikipedia: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Estate_%28Regulation_and_Development%29_Act,_2016) | Read the part on carpet area | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Google Earth versions (web, mobile, Pro desktop)](https://www.google.com/earth/about/versions/) | Open Google Earth (web or mobile) and try the measure tool on your own house or a public ground | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04; check current rules |

## Action task (in your local market)

1. Make a conversion sheet in your workbook with the formulas above and test it on five numbers (10 cents, 4 ares, 1 acre, 1,000 sq m, 2,000 sq ft).
2. With permission, measure your own house plot (or a family plot) with a tape; estimate its area in sq m, ares and cents. Compare with the area in the deed if you have it.
3. Use Google Earth's measure tool on the same plot and compare the three numbers (tape, Google Earth, deed).
4. Find two house listings and work out whether the price per sq ft uses carpet, built-up or super built-up area.

**Proof to record:** Your conversion sheet, the three-way area comparison for one plot and notes on two listings' area basis.

## Template: Area conversion sheet

```
AREA CONVERSIONS (tab "Units")
A2 value | B2 unit | results:
Cents from sq ft:     =A2/435.6
Cents from sq m:      =A2/40.4686
Cents from ares:      =A2*2.47105
Ares from cents:      =A2/2.47105
Sq ft from cents:     =A2*435.6
Sq m from sq ft:      =A2/10.7639
Rectangle (sq m):     =length*width
Trapezium (sq m):     =(side1+side2)/2*width
Triangle (sq m):      =0.5*base*height
PLOT CHECK: tape ___ cents | Google Earth ___ cents | deed ___ cents | difference ___%
```

## Common mistakes

- **Mixing up ares and cents.** An are is about 2.47 cents. Confusing them misprices land by more than double.
- **Comparing prices per sq ft on different area bases.** Ask whether it is carpet, built-up or super built-up.
- **Trusting your own tape measure for legal boundaries.** Only a licensed surveyor's measurement and official records decide.

## Local fraud warning

**Inflated area.** Sellers sometimes quote "about 10 cents" when the deed says 8.4, or include a neighbour's strip, a puramboke edge or a road margin. Always take the area from the deed and the official sketch, and have a surveyor measure if anything doesn't match (RE-M06-L02).

## Quiz

Answer from memory first. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. About how many square feet are in 10 cents?
    - A) 4,356 sq ft
    - B) 435 sq ft
    - C) 43,560 sq ft
    - D) 1,000 sq ft
2. A deed says 8.1 ares. About how many cents is that?
    - A) About 81 cents
    - B) About 20 cents
    - C) About 3.3 cents
    - D) About 8 cents
3. What does super built-up area include?
    - A) Built-up area plus a share of common areas such as stairs and lobbies
    - B) Only the rooms
    - C) Only the land
    - D) Only balconies
4. Who decides a plot's legal measurement in a dispute?
    - A) A licensed surveyor's measurement and the official survey records
    - B) The broker
    - C) Google Earth
    - D) The buyer

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and practise the conversion table
- **Action:** build a conversion sheet and compare tape, Google Earth and deed areas for one plot. It is done when your proof is saved: your conversion sheet, the three-way area comparison for one plot and notes on two listings' area basis.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** 10 × 435.6.
2. **B.** 8.1 × 2.471 ≈ 20.0.
3. **A.** It makes price per sq ft look lower than carpet-area price.
4. **A.** Your estimate is only a check.
